request.query: How many days or weeks did you wait for a DVV appointment for Bank account in Helsinki, and how long until it was done?
request.objective: Forum posts, Reddit threads, blogs and university guides from people who did "Bank account" (DVV) in Helsinki, Finland: how long they waited for an appointment or for the result, and appointment availability.

results.title: Opening a Bank Account in Finland as a Foreigner | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
How long

About 5–10 days from appointment at OP once you have your HETU and documents

...

Opening a bank account in Finland takes longer than in many countries, mostly for two reasons: traditional banks require a henkilötunnus (Finnish personal identity code — your national ID number) and an in-person identity check before they will open a standard account. Realistically, plan for the whole journey — from landing in Finland to having a working account with online codes — to take several weeks, because you also need to complete DVV registration first. A Finnish account is more than a place to park your salary, though: the online banking codes it gives you, the pankkitunnukset ("bank credentials"), double as your digital identity for almost every government and private service in the country. This guide covers what you need, which bank suits a newcomer, what the in-person visit involves, costs and timelines, the rights you have if you are refused, and what to use in the meantime.

...

- Requires a valid passport or national ID, proof of right of residence, and a Finnish address.
- States there is "no workaround" — the henkilötunnus is essential for opening an account and for full online banking.
- Identity is verified in person at a branch. Non-EU citizens may need extra steps (for example a Finnish ID card) to enable strong electronic identification.
- Describes a realistic timeline of roughly 5–10 days once documents are complete (verify on op.fi).

...

Even when you start an application online, all major Finnish banks require an in-person identity-verification visit for a first Finnish account — partly because, until you hold strong electronic identification, you cannot legally sign the documents online. At the branch:

1. Bring every required document — passport or EEA ID card, henkilötunnus, residence document, and proof of address.
2. Identity verification — a bank employee checks and copies your documents and confirms your identity in person.
3. Sign the agreements — you sign the account agreement and the related services agreement.
4. Wait for the post — account details, your debit card, and your online banking codes are typically mailed.

Book the appointment in advance — walk-in service for new account openings is not guaranteed, and at busy branches the wait for a slot can itself add days. For service in English, ask for it when you book; Nordea has a dedicated English line.

...

Timeline. OP describes a realistic 5–10 days from a complete application to a working account, with about a week being the fastest case. But that clock starts only once you have your henkilötunnus and documents — so the full journey from arrival is longer. A sensible mental model: DVV registration and identity code first (often the slowest step), then about a week for the bank, then 1–2 weeks for codes and card by post. Confirm timelines directly with DVV and your bank, as they shift with caseload.

...

How long does it take to open a Finnish bank account?

Once you have your henkilötunnus and documents in order, OP describes a realistic timeline of about 5–10 days, with roughly one week being the fastest if everything is complete (as of 2026 — check op.fi). Add the DVV registration and identity-code wait on top of that, so plan for the whole journey from arrival to take several weeks. Online banking codes and your card typically arrive by post after the branch visit.

results.title: First 30 Days in Finland: The Complete Expat Checklist | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
The henkilötunnus is issued by the DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto, the Digital and Population Data Services Agency) when you register as a foreign national. There are two steps: submit the online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi, then attend an in-person appointment at a DVV service point.

The in-person appointment is the bottleneck. Wait times vary — in Helsinki they can stretch to a few weeks during busy periods. Book the appointment the day you land, even if you submit the form later.

...

Week 2 is the most action-heavy week of the month because the HETU unlocks several parallel tasks.

### Open a Finnish bank account

The three Finnish banks that are most straightforward for new arrivals are OP, Nordea, and Danske Bank. All three require:

- A valid passport or EU identity document
- Your henkilötunnus
- Proof of address (a rental contract or utility bill in your name)
- A reason for needing an account (employment contract or similar)

Book an in-person appointment — walk-ins are rarely accepted. Expect a wait of a few days to a week. During the appointment, the bank will also issue your pankkitunnukset (online banking credentials), which is a separate and critical item covered below.

Until your Finnish account is open, your Wise account handles salary receipts and card spending. Most Finnish retailers accept Visa and Mastercard, so you will not be stuck.

...

DVV appointment wait is too long. DVV service point wait times vary significantly by city. Helsinki is the worst; Espoo, Vantaa, and smaller cities are often faster. If you have flexibility, check DVV's online booking system for all service points within commuting distance and book at whichever has the earliest slot.

...

How long does it take to open a Finnish bank account as a new expat?

You can typically open an account within the first two weeks, once your henkilötunnus has been issued by DVV. OP, Nordea, and Danske Bank all require an in-person appointment and your HETU. Until then, Wise or Revolut can receive your salary and cover daily spending.

results.title: How Long Does It Take to Get a Personal Identity Code in Finland? - Finland Handbook
results.author: Finland Handbook Editorial Team
highlights:
However, for EU citizens or those who didn't receive a code with their permit, the process involves a visit to the DVV. In 2026, the standard processing time for a Personal Identity Code at the DVV is generally 1 to 3 weeks after your appointment. The real challenge is often securing the appointment itself. In major cities like Helsinki, Espoo, or Tampere, the "wait for the wait" can be significant. You might find that the first available slot for identity verification is three weeks away, and only after that does the 1–3 week processing clock begin. Understanding Getting Your Personal Identity Code: The Key to Finnish Healthcare is essential here, as this code is the bedrock of your entire administrative life in Finland.

| Application Path | Typical Processing Time | Key Requirement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residence Permit (Migri) | Linked to permit (1–6 months) | Applied for abroad or at Migri |
| EU Citizen (DVV) | 1–3 weeks after appointment | Valid passport & proof of work/study |
| Nordic Citizen (DVV) | 1 week | Personal appearance at DVV |
| Temporary Worker (Short-term) | 1–2 weeks | Finnish employer's confirmation |

...

While the official estimates give a baseline, the reality on the ground in Finland can vary based on seasonal demand. The "August Rush" is a very real phenomenon. Every year, thousands of international students and new hires arrive simultaneously in late summer. If you submit your request in August or early September, expect the DVV processing times to stretch toward the 4-to-6-week mark. Many newcomers get caught in this cycle, struggling to get their electricity contracts or home internet because the system is simply overwhelmed by the volume of new residents.

...

Furthermore, your location in Finland matters. While Helsinki is the hub, it is also the most congested. If you have the flexibility to travel, sometimes booking an appointment at a DVV office in a smaller town like Porvoo, Lahti, or even further afield can shave weeks off your wait for an appointment. Once the identity verification is done, the digital processing time is relatively uniform across the country, but getting that face-to-face meeting is the primary hurdle. Many people overlook how critical this step is when Registering Your Move (Muuttoilmoitus) with DVV and Posti to ensure their address is correctly linked to their new code.

...

The most pressing question for most is: what do I do while I wait? It feels like life is on hold. You cannot easily get a Finnish bank account, which in turn means you cannot get "Strong Electronic Identification" (bank IDs) to log into government services. During this gap, you are in a state of administrative limbo. For everyday needs, you can often use your foreign passport for basic things, but for services like healthcare, it becomes tricky. Public health centers usually require a Personal Identity Code to create a patient record in their digital systems.

...

To ensure you get your code as fast as possible, you need to be proactive rather than reactive. The moment you know your move-in date, or the moment you receive your residence permit, check the DVV’s online booking system. Do not wait until you land in Finland to see what’s available. Appointments fill up weeks in advance. If you see no appointments in Helsinki, widen your search radius. The train system in Finland is excellent, and a one-hour trip to a neighboring town could save you three weeks of waiting in the city.

results.title: Want to open a bank account in Finland? Don't go to a bank. | Aleksi Linna
results.author: Aleksi Linna
highlights:
If you do that, especially as a non-EU citizen, you'll either get rejected or processed for up to months to get the basic services opened.

...

So, what do you need to do (as a non-EU person)?

First, you must apply for a home municipality at DVV (Digi- ja väestötietovirasto (Finnish Digital Agency).

Depending on your grounds for arriving in Finland, this can take 1 to 10 weeks.

Then, you need to go to a police station to apply for a foreigner's ID card (not a residence permit card), taking another week.

Finally, you go to a bank, and they are happy to open an account and online banking without any extra wait.

results.title: DVV Registration Finland: Get Your Henkilötunnus (2026) | NordicExpat
results.author: Bikram Nath
highlights:
How long

2–3 weeks (work/study) or 3–4 weeks (other cases), from your in-person visit

Where to apply

Online form at dvv.fi, then in person at a DVV service point (Helsinki, Tampere, Turku, Oulu)

...

DVV registration in Finland is how a foreigner enters the Population Information System and receives a henkilötunnus (personal identity code) that banks, the tax office and Kela rely on. You register with the Digital and Population Data Services Agency by submitting an online registration form, then attending one in-person appointment within a month. It is free and takes roughly two to four weeks.

...

Register with DVV in two stages: submit the free online foreigner registration form at dvv.fi/en/foreigner-registration (no authentication needed), then visit a DVV service point in person within 1 month with your passport, residence permit or EU registration certificate, and proof of work or study. Processing then takes 2–3 weeks for work and study cases, 3–4 weeks otherwise. There is no fee — the registration and your henkilötunnus (personal identity code) are completely free.

...

### Step 2 — Book an in-person appointment within one month

After the form, you must visit a DVV service point in person, and you must do so within one month of submitting. The in-person step is non-negotiable — it is where DVV verifies your identity against your documents. Appointments at the busy Helsinki-area locations can fill up, so book as early as you can rather than leaving it to the end of the one-month window.

...

### Step 4 — Wait for processing

Processing time, according to DVV, is roughly 2–3 weeks for work and study registrations and 3–4 weeks for other cases, counted from your visit date. At the end you receive your personal identity code, and DVV separately decides your municipality of residence.

...

Putting it together, a typical sequence for a new arrival looks like this:

1. Before or on arrival — settle your residence basis with Migri (permit for non-EU; right-of-residence registration for EU citizens staying over three months).
2. First days — submit the DVV foreigner registration form online and book the in-person appointment.
3. Within the first month — attend the DVV appointment with your documents; this is also a good moment to use International House Helsinki if you are in the capital region.
4. Weeks two to four — DVV processes the registration (2–3 weeks for work/study, 3–4 weeks otherwise) and assigns your personal identity code and, where eligible, your municipality of residence.
5. Once you have the henkilötunnus — open a Finnish bank account, order a tax card from Vero, and register with Kela.
6. Whenever you move permanently or for over 3 months — file a notification of move within one week.

...

The single most useful thing you can do is start ... Everything downstream — banking, tax, healthcare — is waiting on the code DVV gives you at the end.
